opening.headline: The reason why response time and cost both increased dramatically when the inference strength was increased is explained by dividing it into input, output, and inference tokens.
body: Let's say you change your inference strength to High to improve quality, and your response time multiplies and your monthly costs increase significantly. What's even weirder is that the output tokens on the invoice are much more than the answers you see on the screen. There's something invisible about the cost.

In this lesson, we'll look at what inference tokens the model uses before its answer and how the strength of the inference changes them. Then, after checking the token pre-count method and context limits, we divide the cost into input, output, and inference to determine which terms can be reduced.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of inference strength settings and token calculations
You can decompose the impact of input, output, and inference tokens on cost.

screens.title: When the strength of the inference was increased, the time and cost exploded.
screens.lead: Read the situations below and look for anything unusual in your billing history. There is a difference between the answer shown on screen and the token claimed.

visual.alt: Comparison of token composition bars before and after changing the inference strength.

paragraphs: One team changed the inference strength to high to increase response quality. Since then, response times have multiplied and monthly costs have risen significantly. When I opened the invoice, there were input tokens and output tokens, and the output tokens were much longer than the answer length displayed on the screen. Invisible reasoning was captured as output.

There is something more disappointing. It was only with some requests that the quality actually improved. Even the simplest requests were handled with a high level of intensity, while paying the same price for requests that did not require much thought.
The question we will answer in this lesson is exactly which token the cost comes from. If you look at input, output, and inference separately, you can see where you need to reduce.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Does increasing intensity always increase quality? And what kind of request is it to pay for what you raise?

screens.outro: First, let me recall how I have been calculating costs.

screens.title: Have you ever calculated where your token costs come from?
screens.lead: As you select each box, the instructor's thoughts are revealed. First estimate which box your request will cost the most and then click it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Cell 1: System prompt and conversation history (input)
items.answer: Input tokens come from anything you send with each request, such as system prompts, tool definitions, and conversation history. The longer the conversation goes on, the more the same content is repeated from request to request. This is the most easily visible term.

The output token is proportional to the length of the answer displayed on the screen. This term increases if there are instructions that require you to write a longer answer. Since this term is also visible, it can be estimated relatively easily.

This is an inference token that the model writes internally before answering. Although it does not appear on the screen, it is charged as output and varies greatly depending on the strength of the inference. This is the term that most people leave out of their estimates and is the focus of this lesson.

screens.outro: Let's check what the third column is with explanations for each provider.

screens.title: What is an inference token?
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare how the three providers describe inference tokens and what fields they represent.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI inference models write an internal inference token before creating a response. These tokens are used to make plans and explore alternatives. The documentation explains that depending on the complexity of the problem, there can be hundreds to tens of thousands of inference tokens, and the exact number can be seen in the usage of the response object. `max_output_tokens` is the upper limit of both inference tokens and visible output tokens.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Tokens written to thoughts by Claude are charged as output tokens and are also included in `max_tokens`, even if no thought text is returned. This is also reflected in speed limits. In adaptive thinking, the model dynamically sets the amount of thinking per request, so usage varies from request to request. Even if you receive a summary of your thoughts, the summary is not the entire original reasoning, so the tokens you are charged may be greater than the summary.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Gemini counts `total_thought_tokens` separately in its usage. The example response in the document shows 62 inputs, 171 outputs, and 297 thoughts, for a total of 530. This is a case where there are more tokens written in thought than output that can be seen. This field allows us to see for each request how much was used for inference.

tabs.label: conclusion
tabs.body: For all three providers, invisible inferences are directly factored into costs and delays. So when estimating the cost of an inference model, be sure to check the inference tokens in the Usage field rather than just looking at the length of the answers on the screen. The subject of the next screen is that this value can vary greatly depending on the intensity of the same request.

screens.outro: Now that we know what inference tokens are, let's look at the knob that controls their amount.

screens.title: Reasoning Strength: A knob that determines how deeply you think.
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the strength of your inference. Depending on the value, the same request will have different descriptions of depth of thought, response time, and token usage.

visual.alt: The relationship between inference tokens and response time increases as the inference strength increases.

stops.body: Think lightly and answer quickly. The OpenAI documentation explains that low intensity favors speed and low token usage. It is suitable for simple, delay-sensitive tasks such as classification, and produces the fewest inference tokens.

This is an intermediate step used for most general tasks. Gemini has different basic steps for each model and adjusts the level of thinking with `thinking_level`. Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 default to medium. It's safe to start with this step first, evaluate it, and then adjust it up or down.

Think deeper and consider more alternatives. Most models in Claude default to high, so they use as many tokens as necessary for good results. This is suitable for difficult inferences, but increases both inference tokens and response time. If you use the default for all requests, even simple requests will cost the same.

OpenAI's `reasoning.effort` uses `none`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max` within the range supported by the model. Claude's `output_config.effort` is `max`, `xhigh`, `high`, `medium`, `low`. Claude's effort affects both text, tool call arguments, and thoughts, so it works even if thoughts are turned off. The OpenAI guide recommends starting with low evaluations for delay-sensitive tasks and high for difficult inferences.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to adjust it, let's see how to pre-size it before sending your request.

screens.title: Token Counting and Context Limits
screens.lead: Each time you select the right arrow, input, thought, and output blocks populate the context window. Before sending, check how the sizes are measured and what the limits are.

visual.alt: The context window bar fills with the following order: input, thought, and output.

steps.title: Count input before sending
steps.body: Claude's token counting endpoint reports the number of input tokens before sending messages, including system prompts, tools, images, and PDFs. You can check the input size before actually sending the request.

steps.title: Uses of counting
steps.body: The value counted before sending is used to estimate costs and manage rate limits. Since the calculated value does not include output and thinking, the total cost is determined by adding the expected output and reasoning to it.

steps.title: The context window is a working memory
steps.body: The context window is the model's working memory. System prompts, all messages, tool definitions, as well as output and thoughts all occupy the window. Claude's documentation also explains that precision and recall can decrease with more tokens, so it's important to be selective rather than throw in a lot.

steps.title: Window and output limits by model
steps.body: Claude's latest model supports 1 million token windows and up to 128k output tokens per request. Just because the window is large doesn't mean it has to fill every request. As the input grows, the cost and delay also increase.

steps.title: Input, thoughts, and output are shared
steps.body: Gemini 4's 1 million token window is also shared between input, thought, and output. If the sum of input and `max_output_tokens` exceeds the limit, the output limit is reduced to the remaining space. So keep in mind that increasing your inference strength may require less space in your output.

screens.outro: Now let's break down the three terms separately and analyze where we can reduce them.

screens.title: Analysis: Impact of input, output, and inference tokens on cost
screens.lead: Select the item title to expand it. Break down each of the three terms that make up the cost and see how each term can be reduced.

items.title: input token
items.body: The input token is proportional to the length of the system prompt and conversation history and is repeated for each request. The way to reduce it is to eliminate unnecessary instructions and old conversations. The unit cost of input and output is checked separately in the provider's fee schedule.

items.title: output token
items.body: The output token is proportional to the length of the response visible on the screen. A way to reduce this is to make clear in your instructions the length and format required. Allowing a long description in a request where a single word label would suffice would make this section unnecessarily large.

items.title: inference token
items.body: Inference tokens are charged as output based on the amount of money spent on thinking, and increase as the intensity increases. For the same request, inference tokens can differ significantly between low and high strengths. The way to reduce this is to lower the intensity to match the difficulty of the request. This item is invisible and can only be viewed in the Usage field.

items.title: Sum and Perspective
items.body: Cost is the sum of inputs, outputs, and inferences. Therefore, before reducing, we first check the usage field to see which of the three terms is the largest. If input dominates, organize prompts and history; if inference dominates, check its strength. If you only look at one and reduce it, the other terms will remain the same and the cost will not be reduced significantly. The order of analysis is: measure, find the largest term, adjust, and measure again.

screens.outro: Now that we have a framework for decomposition, let’s solve an example of large waste.

screens.title: Commentary: Waste of high inference strength for simple classification
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the token composition changes. Requests are a simple task that categorizes customer inquiries into three labels: Shipping, Refund, and Other.

states.label: intensity high
states.body: The current setting is inference strength high. The response is a single word label, but there are many more inference tokens than the response. Simple sorting doesn't require deep planning, so this token is mostly useless. Response times become longer, and waste accumulates significantly in services with a large number of requests.

states.label: intensity low
states.body: Decreasing the intensity to low significantly reduces the inference tokens, thus reducing both delay and cost. Claude's guide explains that low is the most efficient for simple tasks, and advises to check whether quality is maintained through evaluation. Therefore, we run several dozen representative inquiries at two levels and compare them to see if the labels are the same, then lower them. By leaving only complex requests at high intensity, you can balance quality and cost. The lesson of this case is not that high intensity is bad in and of itself, but that different requests require different depths. For tasks such as classification, where the correct answer is short and the judgment is simple, low intensity is often sufficient, and only tasks that require multiple levels of reasoning are worth high intensity.

screens.outro: Now that we've finished the case, let's close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Inference strength is a handle on quality, delay, and cost
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Let's find out the answer to the question we asked in the beginning: which token exactly does the cost come from?

paragraphs: To answer the initial question, the cost comes from input tokens, output tokens, and invisible inference tokens. Inference tokens are billed as output even if they are not returned, which explains why the output on the invoice is larger than the answer on the screen.

Inference strength is the knob that moves quality, delay, and cost together. Turning it up is beneficial for thinking through difficult problems, but increases inference tokens and response time, while turning it down makes simple tasks faster and cheaper. Increasing intensity does not always increase quality, so the evaluation is determined according to the difficulty of the request.

Before sending a request, check the input size by token counting and remember that the context window is shared between input, thoughts, and output. To reduce costs, check which of the three terms is larger in the Usage field and adjust from there.

callout.label: distinction to remember
callout.text: Input is the amount sent, output is the visible answer, and inference is the invisible thought. Check the three separately.

glossary.def: This setting determines how deeply the model will think. These include OpenAI's reasoning.effort, Claude's effort, and Gemini's thinking_level.
A token that the model uses for internal inference before answering. You will be charged as output regardless of whether it is returned or not.
This function calculates the number of input tokens before sending a request. Claude has a token counting endpoint.
This is the maximum token range that input, output, and thoughts can occupy together.

misconceptions.myth: There is no charge for invisible inferences.
misconceptions.fact: Claude charges for output tokens even if no thought text is returned, and OpenAI and Gemini also separately count inference tokens in their usage.

misconceptions.myth: Increasing the strength of the inference always increases the quality.
misconceptions.fact: Simple tasks can result in increased costs and delays with virtually no quality. Find out how much strength you need with our assessment.

misconceptions.myth: The context window only counts input.
misconceptions.fact: Output and thoughts also occupy the window. Input, output, and thoughts share the limit.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Inference strength is a knob that controls quality, delay, and cost together.
Inference tokens are charged as output even if they are not visible on the screen.
Token counting allows you to know the input size before sending the request.
Input, output, and inference all share context limits.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which of my requests allow for lower inference strength?

options: The output token of the invoice is the sum of the input tokens
This is because thought summaries are charged separately.
Thoughts that are not returned are also excluded from max_tokens
Tokens spent on thoughts are charged as output regardless of whether they are returned or not.
